heading: Students can be guaranteed to outperform weak supervisors under specific assumptions
definition: conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
summary: Several independent papers derive conditions guaranteeing that students outperform weak supervisors in simplified settings. Evidence comes from theorems and synthetic simulations; applicability to larger models remains unestablished.

suggested_status.by_scale: R2 at toy scale (theorems and synthetic simulations from separate papers). ? at <1B, 1-10B, 10-100B and >100B: no V5 row names a model family or size (counts: versions.V5.studies_by_family = {'other or not stated': 26}; versions.V5.studies_by_size = {'not stated': 26}).
suggested_status.reason: V5 has no original source in the records (counts: versions.V5.original_sources_linked empty). Scripted verdict counts: versions.V5.verdicts.supports.studies 23, versions.V5.verdicts.limits_scope.studies 17, versions.V5.verdicts.challenges.studies 0. Conditional student-over-supervisor guarantees appear across squared-loss regression (arXiv:2405.15116#r20, arXiv:2405.15116#r21), Bregman losses and cross-entropy (arXiv:2501.19105#r27, arXiv:2501.19105#r28), reverse KL (arXiv:2502.11107#R26), and ridgeless linear or random-feature regression (arXiv:2609.33835#R2, arXiv:2609.33835#R8, arXiv:2609.33835#R9). These are different stylized settings; they do not establish reproduction of every specific sufficient condition. The reverse-KL study is T2: it changes the training objective, with forward-loss baselines accompanying that different-method test. Evidence is mostly theorem text (counts: versions.V5.rows_by_evidence_form.text 96, versions.V5.rows_by_evidence_form.figure_only 20, versions.V5.rows_by_evidence_form.table 1). In arXiv:2405.15116 Appendix B, weak error minus misfit can be negative despite positive student error; the authors infer non-negligible Theorem 2 correction terms, not failure of the full corrected bound (arXiv:2405.15116#r21; Appendix B text has no extracted row). For arXiv:2609.33835, continuation assumptions qualify fixed-m and sparse-growing results, and finite-p crossings shift from asymptotic predictions (arXiv:2609.33835#R3, arXiv:2609.33835#R4, arXiv:2609.33835#R5, arXiv:2609.33835#R11, arXiv:2609.33835#R12, arXiv:2609.33835#R14). Its unresolved coverage for part of α > 1 + √2 is untested scope, not a negative result. These corrections retain the proposed R2 at toy scale and do not supply a failed replication warranting C.
suggested_status.open_questions:
1. Does a stated sufficient condition predict student-over-supervisor improvement under full fine-tuning of pretrained language models? A successful or failed replication there would change the assessment above toy scale.
2. Do the misfit and reverse-KL papers share authors? Only overlap with Burns et al. is checked (counts: versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original 0). Confirming independence or overlap would clarify R2 versus R1 for that line.
3. Can the unresolved portion of α > 1 + √2 in arXiv:2609.33835 be covered by proved sign conditions, and do finite-p checks satisfy the stated continuation assumptions?

source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Collin Burns; Pavel Izmailov; J. Kirchner; Bowen Baker; Leo Gao; Leopold Aschenbrenner; Yining Chen; Adrien Ecoffet; Manas R. Joglekar; Jan Leike; I. Sutskever; Jeff Wu

sources.headline: Convex regression students beat weak supervisors by their disagreement with them, up to error terms.
Expansion, fit, and robustness assumptions yield conditions for students to outperform weak supervisors.
Linear-classifier guarantees identify when student error vanishes and when performance stays at chance.
Low-temperature learners provably beat their best expert under specified assumptions about noise or complementary expertise.
Students have guaranteed lower error on difficult examples given well-connected data, agreement, and perturbation resistance.
Kernel regression gains are guaranteed when group proportions match and enough teacher-generated labels are available.
Students reduce teacher variance they do not share, guaranteeing gains when variance dominates error.
ReLU CNN students outperform linear supervisors given thresholds for harmlessly fitting noise and suitable early stopping.
Suitable regularization and alignment give students lower error in the limit than insufficiently regularized teachers.
Convex students representing targets exactly reduce cross-entropy by student–teacher KL divergence, up to approximation terms.
Representations that split into components provide sufficient conditions for students to outperform weak supervisors.
Reverse KL guarantees convex students representing targets exactly improve by their disagreement with teachers.
Under specified training conditions, logistic-regression students align better with the target than either supervising teacher.
Spectral assumptions guarantee random-feature students outperform teachers, with the fraction of performance gap recovered approaching one.
Students approximating teachers’ posterior averages can achieve lower risk under conditions involving Bregman divergence.
Linear regression gives exact improvement conditions even when students and teachers have no difference in capacity.
Random-feature ridge regression theory shows when students improve on teachers, though they cannot outperform optimal teachers.
Well-aligned PCA initializations enabled students to outperform weak supervisors in synthetic experiments.
Stopping appropriately guarantees quadratic or polynomial student performance gains if Gaussian-data predictions hold for other distributions.
Positive alignment guarantees gains in early-stopped logistic regression even with equal student and teacher capacity.
Early-stopped regression students provably outperform teachers given enough data and assumptions about the feature spectrum.
Reverse KL students gain by their disagreement with teachers, matching predictions in synthetic experiments.
TreeDPO preference training guarantees gains over strong supervised fine-tuning, assuming a relationship between loss and performance.
Biased weak supervision sets a minimum bias in plain fine-tuning; noisy supervision limits learning efficiency.
On finite-sample molecular benchmarks, the student–teacher disagreement bound fails when error terms are omitted.
Uniform expert imitation cannot outperform the best expert without temperature changes.
Mismatched group proportions can prevent gains regardless of how many model-generated labels are available.
Students’ advantage over teachers can vanish when bias or approximation error outweighs variance reduction.
Students may not outperform already optimally regularized teachers, or when insufficiently aligned with the target.
Student–teacher disagreement overstates measured gains for unrepresentable targets; ImageNet lacks the predicted trend across head counts.
Errors from finite samples and approximation can erase reverse-KL guarantees of student improvement.
Students with optimal shrinkage regularization cannot improve near-chance teachers, even through repeated distillation.
For nucleus segmentation, students’ theoretical error bound exceeds teachers’ own error and therefore cannot guarantee improvement.
Continuation assumptions and finite-dimensional threshold shifts qualify asymptotic regression guarantees.
Bounds for general divergence measures need extra assumptions to guarantee student improvement.
In synthetic tests, students outperform supervisors from initializations beyond the conservative region covered by theory.
Targets with mixed components and unsuitable stopping weaken or eliminate predicted quadratic gains in student performance.
Polynomial students reveal target features while preserving others, without aligning with targets better than weak supervisors.
The early-stopping guarantee covers gains over the starting model and weakens as student weight magnitudes grow.
In general classification, gains cannot exceed the square root of student–teacher disagreement.

wording_issues.issue: The results are conditional guarantees. Several give only sufficient conditions (2405.16043, 2502.00620 untested-parts lines). Some hold with high probability (2503.02877 R1–R3, 2605.05742 R1, 2507.06187 r30), others only asymptotically (2505.18346 limiting errors, 2609.33835 deterministic equivalents), or up to error terms that on real data can swamp the gain (2502.11107 R27; 2405.15116 text). A few papers give iff or necessary conditions (2610.09044 r8; 2603.05691 r6; 2609.33835).

The comparator varies. TreeDPO's conditional theorem compares with strong SFT, whose ordering relative to the weak supervisor is not established; literal V5 is cannot_determine, and the proof uses the posited loss–performance relationship in Equation 13 (2507.18858 r44). Early-stopped logistic regression directly guarantees improvement over the initial student, which also beats the teacher when the student starts stronger (2605.05742 R1). Two-layer polynomial networks with an even target link establish target-feature elicitation and off-target preservation under the stated assumptions; this supports feature-level surpassing, while superior target-task reward performance remains unestablished (2605.12908 R1–R2). The expert-mixture theory compares with the best constituent expert: Proposition 3 mixes optimal predictions with uniform random outputs; Proposition 4 requires experts optimal on disjoint subsets and uniformly random elsewhere, with test mass on at least two subsets (2406.11741 r9).

No V5 row is on a named model family (counts: versions.V5.studies_by_family = {'other or not stated': 26}). Students are ridge or ridgeless regressors (2505.18346), random-feature networks (2503.02877), minimum-norm-interpolating linear classifiers (2410.04638) and two-layer networks. Supervisors include human chess players (2406.11741) and SAM (2512.11722 R13). The weak-model-supervises-larger-LM setup of V1 isn't what these theorems model.

The statement names no condition and doesn't separate sufficient from necessary ones. The studies give distinct condition families. Misfit or disagreement under convexity and realizability (2405.15116, 2502.11107). Expansion (2405.16043). Low teacher–student similarity or feature overlap (2509.24005 R1, 2502.05075 r2). Early stopping in a window (2610.09044 r4). A sub-optimal teacher (2505.18346 R2, 2603.05691 r4). A wider student (2609.33835 Remark 5.5).

method_sensitivity.what: Under convexity and realizability, reverse KL gives student error ≤ weak error − disagreement (2502.01458 R17); forward KL needs an extra weighted Itakura–Saito condition (R19). Synthetic reverse-KL (R20–R22) and forward-KL (R23–R25) points lie around y = x. In the realizable settings (R20, R23), the strong representation equals the 16-layer ground-truth MLP; the weak representation is a pre-trained 2-layer MLP. The reverse-CE bound assumes convexity and realizability and carries ½ and + log k (2502.11107 R28). General f-divergence bounds give no guaranteed gain (2506.03109 TH1–TH3).

For the random-feature student with α > k0, γ < k0 gives LST ≍ 1 while LTE ≍ d^(-(α−k0)) → 0: the student is asymptotically worse (r3). k0 ≤ γ < (α+k0)/2 gives LST ≍ LTE²; at γ = (α+k0)/2, a (log d)² factor can appear, so quadratic scaling is qualified by polylogarithmic factors (r4). (α+k0)/2 < γ < α gives an improvement exponent between 1 and 2 (r5). γ ≥ α gives LST ≍ LTE (r6) (2610.09044). 2503.02877 reports early stopping is crucial and overtraining makes the student mimic the teacher. 2605.05742 reports that training past the peak hurts. 2606.01292 reports an intermediate optimal training stage.

Standard ridge: the outcome flips with teacher regularization λt relative to σε²γt (R1 vs R2, R3), the student's λs interval, and eq. 5 for over-parameterized students (R3 vs R4) (2505.18346). Random-feature ridge regression: improvement regions differ for variance-dominated (r4) and bias-dominated (r5) teachers, and there is no exponent gain over an optimally tuned teacher (r7) (2603.05691).

In 2609.33835 Case I, the proportional-regime critical threshold applies for 2 < α ≤ 1 + √2: improvement holds for mcrit < m < p (R2). For 1 < α ≤ 2, every fixed proportional ratio 0 < m/p < 1 gives positive limiting gain. In the fixed-m regime, for 1 < α < 2 and 0 < σ² < σc², Gm < 0 near m = 1 (R3); these results require continuation assumptions. m ≥ p gives W2SG = 0 (R6). 2510.24812 has different guarantees for data-scarce (R4, R5) and data-abundant (R6) regimes. 2509.24005 needs enough pseudolabels (small νz, R1). 2502.05075's variance reduction needs N > ds (r2).

The gain grows as teacher–student similarity falls (2509.24005 R1). The student inherits teacher variance only in the shared feature subspace (2502.05075 r2). Under Assumption 3.7 and the stated regularization conditions, PredGap = ∥Ps(I−Pw)(ŷ/√n̂)∥² ± o(1), with high probability (2502.00620 r1). 2605.05742's condition (ii) needs student and teacher poorly correlated in directions orthogonal to θ*, since similar errors make ρ small (not in rows).

method_sensitivity.factor: initialization / pre-training alignment and learning rate
method_sensitivity.what: Synthetic single-index runs: initial alignment τ = 0.1 fails (R4) and τ ≥ 0.7 succeeds (R5). A poor but still warm initialization succeeds at learning rates 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻³; Appendix C.3 prose gives ρ = 0.4, while Figure 8's legend gives ρ = 0.3 (R10). This demonstrates conservative sufficient conditions rather than failure of a necessary warm-start condition. Above ~10⁻², error spikes to ≈ 1.4, above the weak baseline (R12) (2605.05710). Weighted ridge: small alignment ζ fails (R6) and larger ζ beats an optimally regularized teacher (R7) (2505.18346).

For the random-feature student with target degree k0 ∈ {0,1} ∪ 2N, α > k0 gives LST ≍ LTE² at T = (log m + log(LTE^(-1)))/σk0² (r1); 0 < α ≤ k0 gives LTE ≍ LST ≍ 1 and no improvement (r2) (2610.09044). In two-layer polynomial networks, under target-subspace concentration and off-target-localization assumptions, even target links permit target-feature elicitation with off-target preservation (2605.12908 R1, R2); odd target links with GE = 1 produce off-target drift and forgetting (Remark 2). This guarantee concerns features, without establishing reward-quality superiority. Matched versus mismatched group proportions affect gains: ηu = ηℓ (R1) versus ηu ≠ ηℓ (R2) (2509.24005). In IMDb, correction happens on class 0 but not class 1 (2405.16043 method-sensitivity line).

Without a temperature change, an idealized learner fitting a uniform expert mixture never beats the best expert (r7). Argmax superiority is equivalent to exceeding every expert at all sufficiently low temperatures (r8). Sufficient settings (r9) are: a single expert follows the optimal predictor except that, with probability 0 < ρ < 1, it samples uniformly over all outputs; or experts are optimal on their respective disjoint subsets and uniformly random elsewhere, with positive test probability on at least two subsets. Here ρ is the random-output probability (2406.11741).
